processing: Little is documented about how it is made. It is treated as a green tea, like most Mount Emei teas, and its fine, downy strips suggest a tender picking.
harvest_season: Not well documented; spring would be usual for a tender Mount Emei green.
appearance_dry: Tight, fine strips with visible white down, said to look like flower stamens.
appearance_liquor: Not well documented; a pale yellow-green would be typical of a tender Sichuan green.
appearance_wet: Not well documented; small, tender leaves and buds would be typical of the style.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting description exists for this tea in particular; tender Mount Emei greens are generally fresh, light and clean.

brewing.notes: General advice for a fine, downy green: cooler water, a short first steep, and expect a little haze from the down.

vintage_note: How it is sold today is not well documented. Assuming it follows other Mount Emei greens, buy the current spring's harvest and drink it within a year.
description:
E Rui is a Mount Emei tea whose name joins the first character of Emei with the word for a flower's stamen or pistil. That name is said to come from the look of the leaf: tight, fine strips covered in white down.

It is linked with the mountainside around the White Dragon Cave and Black Water Temple. Beyond this, little is documented, including exactly how it is made or who makes it now.

As with other tender green teas of Mount Emei, you would expect something fresh and light, and cool water is the safe way to brew it. Treat that as a guide to the class rather than a tasting note for this tea.

If you find it on sale, ask for the harvest year and the place of production, since this name is uncommon compared with neighbours such as Zhu Ye Qing or Emei Xueya.
history: Little is firmly documented. A 2013 Chinese newspaper piece cites an old Mount Emei gazetteer and says the tea was a tribute over a thousand years ago, a claim best taken as tradition. No clear modern record of its development or producers has surfaced.
